item.title: Anthropic faces challenges once it goes public on Wall Street
item.description: When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops AI.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence. The San Francisco startup, which plans an initial public offering this month, has sketched out a governance structure that it says will protect the company’s broader mission against the pull of financial interests. But the mechanisms it describes give the company wide leeway to decide how to measure whether it’s benefiting society, experts say. Like its rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory. “I think then the real test emerges if and when the question of public benefit becomes costly” — or when the public benefit comes into conflict with making a profit, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of Cornell University’s Tech Policy Institute. In its regulatory filings, Anthropic pledges to pursue long-term benefits of humanity through the responsible development of advanced AI. “We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings,” the company said. Anthropic also has pledged at least five per cent of its stock to a “public benefit” fund and its founders have committed to donate 80 per cent of their wealth. A pledge to do good is baked into corporate structure Other tech companies have pledged to do good including Google, which prominently featured its then-motto, “Don’t Be Evil,” in its investor prospectus when it went public in 2004. But the words were not legally binding, and critics have accused the tech giant of leaving them behind. Elon Musk’s takeover of Twitter in 2022 shows how the conflict between profit and public good might play out in real life, said Stavros Gadinis, a law professor at UC Berkeley School of Law. “Let’s say that Twitter’s directors felt that Elon was the wrong guy to police the public square because they didn’t trust him, they didn’t like him, they didn’t think he’d be fair, whatever it was,” Gadinis said. “But he made them an offer that was so high compared to what their advisors told them the company was really worth that it would be against their fiduciary duties to not sell to Elon. This is the situation that the public benefit charter is trying to avoid.” Had Twitter been a public benefit corporation, it could have been required to consider factors beyond maximizing shareholder value when selling the company. There aren’t many public benefit corporations whose shares are publicly traded and they are all much smaller than Anthropic and OpenAI. They include the eyewear company Warby Parker, the insurance company Lemonade and software developer Veeva Systems, which had a conventional corporate structure when it went public in 2013 and converted to a public benefit corporation in 2021. Anthropic’s idealistic ambitions for how it develops AI could run up against competitive pressure, such as from China, Kreps said. Anthropic and OpenAI’s models have gone from answering almost any question, even if it was dangerous, to becoming much more circumspect. But as they face more competition, including from open-source Chinese models that likely will tell you whatever you want, she said, “will they start to rethink some of those guardrails? And what happens then?” The setup generally is not preferred by shareholders because it gives more power to the company’s board than it does to shareholders. Whatever a company decides as its public benefit mission, it will likely be much more difficult to measure than profits. That’s particularly true for AI companies, whose leaders have exalted AI as the solution to many of humanity’s problems — from curing cancer to creating economic prosperity. “There are these echo chambers, the Silicon Valley bubble where they really think that what they’re doing is for the good of humanity,” Kreps said. And someone immersed in that environment, she added, might not even ask the right questions or understand how “public benefit” should be measured. A trust aims to hold Anthropic accountable A Long-Term Benefit Trust created by Anthropic is intended to operate as an independent body of trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Through a special Class T common stock, the trust “generally has the authority to elect and remove” Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of Anthropic’s board of directors, according to the IPO filing. The Class T common stock is a single share that allows the five trustees to vote as a unit. It has no economic rights — meaning they get to vote but they don’t see any financial benefit or losses from the share and can’t sell it. “The LTBT’s arrangements are designed to minimize the LTBT’s and the Trustees’ exposure to our financial performance and grant the Trustees sufficient independence to ensure we are striking this balance appropriately,” the filing said. Three of the company’s board directors are elected by the trust directly, and another three are elected by other shareholders, which include the company founders with a 50.1 per cent voting majority. A seventh director, with a potentially tie-breaking vote, is nominated by the trust and the holders of the Class T shares, but cannot be appointed or removed without consent from the board’s nominating committee, which is expected to be controlled by the founders. Effectively, the trust can only hold Anthropic accountable on issues such as AI safety and the company’s broader mission up to a point, Gadinis said. The trust “cannot determine the everyday decisions of these directors or the management of the company,” he said. ”If they disagree, they will have to go through the effort of removing directors, and they may not be able to remove a majority.” As a public company, Anthropic also will be required to report finances and generally be more transparent than a privately held one. Many public companies dealing with AI, including Google and Microsoft, regularly update the public on efforts to develop AI responsibly. The incentive for transparency could be as powerful as other mechanisms set up in Anthropic’s corporate structure, Gadinis said. “I do think that by being public, we are going to get a lot more information, because a lot of people are going to be asking questions, and companies will be responding to these questions. Not only because they’re required by security laws, but also because they want to build this kind of trust with the investing community,” he said. --- Barbara Ortutay, The Associated Press

item.title: Nvidia forecasts quarterly revenue above estimates in first report since Huang’s exit as CEO
item.description: Nvidia forecast quarterly revenue above Wall Street estimates, giving investors some relief after Jensen Huang’s resignation plunged the chipmaker into crisis.
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: Nvidia forecasts quarterly revenue above Wall Street estimates on Tuesday, giving investors some relief after longtime leader Jensen Huang’s resignation plunged the chipmaker into crisis. The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of US$130.0 billion, plus or minus three per cent, compared with analysts’ average estimate of US$125.25 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. Nvidia said it did not assume any data centre chip sales from China in its outlook. With Huang gone, investors are looking for clues about Nvidia’s future, from billions of dollars invested in cloud providers, suppliers and AI startups to who will ultimately lead the world’s most valuable chipmaker. The AI boom’s most prolific salesman resigned on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees. U.S. intelligence agencies are trying to determine the extent of her ties to China’s Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two people familiar with the matter. Huang’s exit ended three decades of founder-led control over Nvidia’s chip roadmap, customer deals and Washington ties, making execution a bigger risk than near-term AI demand, analysts say. Finance chief Colette Kress is interim CEO, while the board considers internal and external candidates. A growing “Stand With Jensen” campaign has complicated the search, although the board is not considering Huang’s return, three people told Reuters on Monday. Huang said on Tuesday he would be “honored” to return if the board deemed it best. Earlier on Tuesday, Nvidia’s board created a committee on national security and export controls, its first major governance move since Huang’s departure, as scrutiny grows over the chipmaker’s national security role. Washington has also tightened licensing rules for chip shipments to Southeast Asia and overseas data centres serving Chinese firms, while lawmakers prepare to question Huang, who had pushed for greater chip exports to China. Investors were already uneasy about AI spending after Democrats’ midterm sweep fueled fears of tougher scrutiny and slower data-centre expansion. They also want to know whether Nvidia’s next CEO will continue financing customers, a practice critics call circular. Tuesday’s results offer a first read on Vera Rubin, Nvidia’s newest generation of AI processors and successor to Grace Blackwell. Nvidia said in August that Vera Rubin would account for about a fifth of data centre revenue in the October quarter and forecast 70 per cent revenue growth in the next fiscal year. --- Reporting by Anhata Rooprai in Bengaluru; Editing by Shinjini Ganguli and Anil D’Silva

item.title: Telus sees ‘serious concerns’ with Quebecor’s $31B takeover bid
item.description: Quebecor Inc. is proposing a strategic combination with Telus Corp. in a cash-and-stock deal valued at about $31 billion.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: MONTREAL — The chief executive of Quebecor Inc. says his company’s proposed $31-billion takeover of Telus Corp. is meant to drive efficiencies and free up cash to spend on new infrastructure, while dismissing concerns that a merger would lead to deteriorating competition in the telecommunications sector. Quebecor revealed Monday it is proposing the merger with Telus in a cash-and-stock deal. The Montreal-based company said a potential deal would combine complementary networks, spectrum and operations to boost investment capacity and create a more competitive company. “Our transaction is not based on increasing revenues, it’s certainly not based on increasing prices,” said Quebecor president and CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau in an interview. “Our transaction is to generate savings, to generate synergies that will be able for us ... to reduce the amount of debt, but also to make sure that we will have the financial resources to invest in other networks.”  Péladeau said the Canadian telecom sector is vulnerable to the threat of foreign players taking market share. He pointed to American companies like SpaceX, whose satellite internet service known as Starlink has been gaining ground in Canada as it poaches customers from established providers. “If we were not to have Canadian operators that are financially strong, ... we should think about what’s going to happen down the road. In the meantime, it’s time to do something,” Péladeau said. “When you’re joining those companies together ... you’re going to be able maybe to take those financial resources and invest in another type of network which is also going to be the network of the future.” Quebecor estimates the proposed takeover would create around $160 million in annual operating cost savings and $235 million in annual capital savings, on top of Telus’ recently announced goal of achieving approximately $900 million in savings per year moving forward from the end of 2028. It said those efficiencies would support new spending on network upgrades, integration with Canadian satellite networks and service enhancements. It would also go toward the deployment of artificial intelligence, data centres and advanced connectivity infrastructure. But Telus chief executive Victor Dodig said in an interview that the company has “serious concerns” with Quebecor’s proposal, with the “largest hurdle” being regulatory issues.  He said the offer also “doesn’t nearly reflect the value of Telus.” “I think this is all about the resilience, strength, sovereignty and safety of the telecom sector in Canada. This does not advance that at all,” said Dodig, who took the helm at Telus in July. Telus said its board of directors has formed a special committee of independent directors to review and evaluate the Quebecor proposal and explore other strategic alternatives. Asked about Quebecor’s goal of finding savings so that a potential combined company could spend more on infrastructure and new technologies, Dodig said that’s something his company already has “completely under control.” “In my estimation, every single point of their offer has serious complications,” he said. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said in a statement on Monday that the transaction will be “rigorously reviewed.” “We will not predetermine the outcomes of the reviews related to this or any other specific transaction,” the statement said.  “In the face of accelerating technological change, global instability and ongoing cost-of-living pressures, the Government of Canada will relentlessly prioritize the best interests of Canadians and Canadian sovereignty.” Quebecor said it made a non-binding proposal to Telus on June 26 to serve as the basis for negotiations and then submitted what it called an “enhanced proposal” on Nov. 9. Under the offer, Telus shareholders would receive $6.35 in cash and 0.17 class B shares of Quebecor for each Telus share. Quebecor said the bid is worth $19.45 per share based on its closing share price on Friday. Telus shares closed at $12.14 on Friday. Despite Dodig arguing the offer undervalues Telus, Péladeau said he believes the offer is fair based on the company’s share price. “The market is valuing their shares at $12. It’s not me, it’s the market,” he said. “I mean (Dodig’s) been there for what, three, four months now, even more? In fact, the stock went further down than up.” Scotiabank analyst Maher Yaghi said a potential deal would face significant obstacles, pointing to likely reviews by the Competition Bureau, the CRTC and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada. He said additional federal reviews or approvals could also be required “given the strategic nature of Canadian telecommunications infrastructure.” Telus noted that even if such a deal received regulatory approvals, it may be subject to certain conditions that “materially affect the combined company.”  If a merger between Quebecor and Telus moved forward, it would be the largest takeover in Canada’s telecom sector since Rogers Communications Inc. purchased Shaw in 2023. As part of that $26-billion transaction, Quebecor’s Videotron subsidiary acquired Freedom Mobile from Shaw. Rogers and Shaw agreed to sell Freedom to Videotron to ease competition concerns raised by the original proposal. Both of those transactions came with a list of conditions meant to protect competition in the telecom sector. They included Rogers establishing a second headquarters in Calgary and adding 3,000 new jobs based in Western Canada that it must maintain for at least 10 years. Rogers was also required to spend billions to expand 5G coverage and additional network services, as well as to connect rural, remote and Indigenous communities. Dodig said Telus is drawing lessons from the Rogers-Shaw merger, which took more than two years to come to fruition after it was initially proposed as the companies involved worked to address government and regulatory concerns. “We’re all modernizing our businesses, our way of life. The telecom sector and Telus’ role in it needs to kind of stay at the forefront, not get caught up in some sort of regulatory morass that’s going to take years,” Dodig said. As part of the Rogers-Shaw merger, Videotron was required to offer plans at least 20 per cent lower than its competitors and spend $150 million over two years to upgrade Freedom Mobile’s network. It is also restricted from transferring any Freedom Mobile licences for a decade. Quebecor said that it “has fully performed the undertakings it made” to Ottawa since that deal, while demonstrating its ability “to combine growth, pro-consumer pricing and innovation.” It noted that wireless prices fell 35.4 per cent in the three years following the acquisition of Freedom, according to Statistics Canada. “Of all the obligations we took, we even delivered them faster. There’s no reason we will change. Our track record is there to show what we are able to do,” Péladeau said. “If we were to take other obligations, we’ll listen to ISED, we’ll listen to the (Competition) Bureau and we will do what is appropriate to make sure that we will be then generating resources that will make this company and this country stronger.” Péladeau said Quebecor has discussed the potential merger with federal regulators and planned to meet with Dodig next Monday to discuss further steps. But combining two of Canada’s four largest wireless service providers “would undo the competitive structure regulators set up when they required Freedom to be divested as part of the Rogers-Shaw approval,” Scotiabank’s Yaghi said in a note. “Without meaningful remedies, the deal runs against the government policy intent behind the Freedom transaction,” he said, adding that approval could be contingent on Quebecor offering “significant concessions to the government” to keep telecom prices low. “Regulatory decisions will make or break the deal, not price. If Quebecor is not ready to let go of Freedom Mobile, we believe this deal has a low chance of going through.” Quebecor’s share price fell about 15 per cent or $11.81 to $65.25 in trading on Monday. Telus’ share price was up about 13 per cent or $1.56 to $13.70. --- Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.
